# Notes Before the Concept Meeting

*Written before the tasting panels, deliberately. Concepts assembled after the panel results are not concepts. They're a summary of what tested least badly among the things we happened to think of.*

---

## What we're actually developing

The brief says flavours for a local palate. The brief is slightly wrong, or at least it's leading with the part that's easiest to talk about.

Flavour is the most copyable thing in this business. Any competent local manufacturer can reverse-engineer a seasoning blend in about eight weeks, and they have a cost base we won't match and a grandmother-adjacent credibility we can't buy. If our advantage is the recipe, we've entered a fight we lose slowly and expensively.

What is *not* copyable in eight weeks: a format nobody else is making, a price architecture the incumbents' plants can't hit, a supply relationship for an ingredient that has no organised export market, and a distribution habit we own — which snack is in whose hand, at which hour, for which reason.

So I'd treat flavour work as necessary and visible — it's how we demonstrate we're serious and it's what the market research is equipped to measure — and quietly spend the real effort on occasion, format, and shelf. That ordering is the substance of these notes. Everything below is downstream of it.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

The brief says "target international market," which is a phrase doing a lot of hiding. I'm going to write as though we mean Indonesia, because it's the case where my reasoning is most testable and because being wrong in a specific direction is more useful than being vague in the right one. If somebody in the room knows we mean Vietnam, or Saudi, or Mexico, this is the moment where saying so is cheap. Most of the structure transfers; roughly a third of the specifics don't.

Worth noting what makes it the interesting case: a very young population, an extraordinarily high snacking frequency, a retail landscape still dominated by hundreds of thousands of small independent outlets, a coin-denominated price ceiling per unit, a climate that destroys crispness, and a palate that treats sweet and savoury as a continuum rather than two rooms.

---

## What the research can and can't tell us

"Demand for new and interesting options" is a finding I'd handle carefully. It is almost always true, everywhere, and it is almost always a description of what people say rather than what they buy. Novelty appetite in snacks is real but it is *trial* appetite — high first purchase, brutal repeat rates. A product line designed to satisfy stated curiosity is a product line of one-and-done SKUs.

The more useful question, which I'd put to the research team as a suggestion rather than a correction: what are people currently doing with their hands and mouths at 4pm, at 10pm, on a motorbike, in a shared car, waiting outside a school, during the last hour before dawn in Ramadan? And which of those moments is currently being served by something *inadequate*? Novelty sells a bag. An inadequately served occasion sells a habit.

---

## Ideas, grouped by the bet each one makes

I'd float all of these rather than propose any. Some are more defensible than others and I'd be interested to see which ones people gravitate to unprompted, because that tells me something about the room.

**1. The one-handed line — a bet on the commute.**
Enormous volumes of daily life happen on a motorbike or in a jam. The unmet requirement isn't flavour, it's engineering: no grease transfer to fingers, no crumb, no bag that needs two hands, no shard that fragments in a helmet. Something like a firm coated cluster or a compressed stick in a rigid single-file sleeve you can operate with a thumb. Savoury-sweet coating, low friability. The insight worth protecting here is mechanical, not culinary, which means it's harder to copy and easier to patent than a sambal.

**2. The nongkrong format — a bet on the group.**
Consumption is frequently communal and unhurried: several people, one table, hours. Western portioning assumes an individual. A large, low-density, deliberately low-cost sharing format designed to be poured onto a plate at a warung or café — with two or three seasoning sachets included so the group can argue about heat level — turns the snack into a small social event rather than a purchase. Sachets also let us ship one base product against several taste segments, which is a manufacturing argument disguised as a fun idea.

**3. The sour-savoury axis — a bet that we've been mapping heat and missing the real variable.**
Everyone localising into the region reaches for chilli. Chilli is table stakes and it's where the incumbents are strongest. The more interesting territory is acid and aromatic freshness: tamarind, calamansi, lime leaf, raw shallot and lemongrass in the *sambal matah* register, green chilli rather than red. Also the "doesn't make you thirsty, doesn't scratch the throat" property, which people describe unprompted and which no Western brief has ever contained. That's a formulation target: salt and MSG management, oil level, coating adhesion. If we can honestly claim it, we have a benefit statement nobody else is making.

**4. The sweet-savoury collapse — a bet against our own category boundaries.**
Cheese with sugar. Chocolate with cheese. Sweetcorn as a savoury flavour and as a milk flavour. Condensed milk as a legitimate topping for something salty. Pandan, taro, jackfruit, black glutinous rice — dessert flavours applied to crisp savoury bases. Our internal instinct will be that these are wrong. That instinct is the local competitive advantage of anyone who doesn't have it.

**5. The Ramadan and Lebaran architecture — a bet on the calendar.**
This is the one I'd argue hardest for, sideways. Two distinct occasions the category mostly ignores: the pre-dawn meal, which wants something dense, less thirst-inducing, mildly sweet, dates-adjacent, and the gifting season, which wants tins, assortments, presentation, and a price point that carries social meaning. A seasonal gifting SKU can carry a disproportionate share of annual margin and, more importantly, buys us shelf negotiation leverage the rest of the year. It also fails safely: seasonal products are allowed to be discontinued without anyone's career ending.

**6. The tempe platform — a bet on sourcing as moat, and possibly a reverse export.**
Fermented soy, cassava, melinjo, banana, and small dried fish are all local raw materials with fragmented supply and no serious international demand competing for them. Building a genuine procurement and quality-control relationship there is slow, unglamorous, and structurally hard to replicate — which is exactly why it's worth doing. Secondary possibility, offered lightly because it will sound like empire-building: a fermented-soy protein crisp with a real protein number is a product our home markets are currently trying and failing to invent. The interesting version of this project may end up flowing the other direction.

**7. The imported-cue premium — a bet on segmentation, held loosely.**
For a minority of urban consumers, visible foreign origin is the benefit. This argues for a small premium tier that *doesn't* localise — that stays legibly what we are — sitting alongside the localised mainstream line. Worth two SKUs and no more, because it's a hedge, not a strategy, and because it's the kind of idea that expands to fill whatever attention it's given.

---

## The constraint I'd design from, not to

Start from the coin. If the dominant unit of purchase in the independent trade is a single small pack at a price point set by what's in a pocket, then that price is not a marketing decision made at the end. It's the first line of the formulation brief. Ingredient cost, coating weight, film specification, and case count all fall out of it, and any concept that can't survive it is a concept for a supermarket-only product — which is a different, smaller, more crowded business than the one we said we were entering.

Two related things I'd want somebody to own from week one rather than discover in month nine:

Humidity. Crispness in an unairconditioned outlet at high ambient humidity for the full shelf life is a barrier-film and water-activity problem that will constrain flavour delivery more than any panel result. Solve it early or watch it silently veto our best ideas late.

Halal certification, and the equivalent question in whichever market we actually mean. Drawn once, early, quietly, and treated as an external condition of entry rather than as a topic — because a condition can be engineered around, whereas a topic gets re-opened under time pressure by someone with a deadline and a flavour they love.

---

## What I'd do first

Not a launch. A small, ugly, deliberately over-reaching test: four or five concepts, including at least two that our own people find slightly wrong, placed in real independent outlets in one city, at the real price, in the real climate, with someone physically watching who buys and whether they come back within a fortnight. Repeat rate at fourteen days is the only number I'd let into the second meeting.

And I'd manufacture one early argument on purpose — put the cheese-and-sugar concept in front of the regional distributor and the home-market brand team in the same week and watch how the disagreement resolves. If the whole development process has been frictionless, we've learned nothing about which of these ideas anyone will actually defend when it gets difficult.

---

## Tests fixed now, before the evidence arrives

Because criteria written afterwards are commentary.

There is at least one element per SKU that isn't a recipe — a format, a supply relationship, a shelf-life property — that a local competitor cannot reproduce inside a quarter.

Each concept survives the price point of the dominant retail unit, not the supermarket one.

Each concept can be described by a nineteen-year-old to a friend in one clause, in the local language, without our help.

Repeat purchase at two weeks, not trial, is the gate. Anything that clears trial and fails repeat is a novelty, and I'd rather kill three novelties in month two than defend one in year two.

At least two of the surviving concepts are things we currently think are wrong.

---

The failure mode here isn't picking a bad flavour. It's that by month six the line exists as a fact inside our own organisation — with a sponsor, a name, a slot in the plan — and the case for launching has quietly become the case for not having wasted the year.

The defence isn't discipline. It's having kept a genuinely different concept alive in parallel the whole way through, so that when the moment comes there's somewhere else to go and it doesn't have to be invented in a meeting.

We aren't designing snacks for a foreign palate. We're buying a place in somebody's afternoon, from someone who currently has that place and doesn't know they're at risk.
